summary:
Paraguay has no legal gender recognition procedure in force. The judiciary has yet to issue final rulings in ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda that have been pending since 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and are awaiting a decision. A 1993 civil court case seeking to register Ramón Fidel, who had undergone gender reassignment surgery, as a woman ended without a decision because Fidel died in a traffic accident before judgment. Trans people are not permitted to change their name or gender on official documents, so a trans visitor whose passport marker conflicts with their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.

Amnesty International's 2025-26 reporting records two trans migrants who were denied identity documents, evidence that the documentary gap reaches administrative encounters rather than staying theoretical.

Health settings are the one area where a chosen name is formally recognised. Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare Resolution 695, approved in October 2016, provides that trans people may use their social name on medical records, medical histories and forms, and requires officials in the Integrated Networks of Health Services to assist and treat trans patients using the name with which they identify. Law 7018 on Mental Health, enacted 15 November 2022, provides in Article 3 that mental-health care is governed by non-discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and that a diagnosis may in no case be made solely on the basis of sexual choice, sexual orientation or gender identity.

Official hostility toward trans people is documented at the national and municipal levels. In October 2017 the government imposed a ban on discussion of LGBT issues in public schools, and the Minister of Education said the ministry might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Asunción's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March. Horacio Cartes, a leading figure of the ruling party, said he would shoot himself in the testicles if his son married another man, later apologising to those offended.

Discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns and into internal and cross-border migration and into sex work, according to reporting from September 2025. Violence and discrimination against LGBT people are frequent and often ignored by police. Amnesty International counted 37 registered feminicides in 2025, a figure not disaggregated for trans victims, and in April a bill was introduced to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family.

No broad anti-discrimination law covers Paraguay. A bill introduced in November 2015 to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced since introduction, and violence and discrimination against LGBT people are frequently left unaddressed by police, leaving a visitor who is targeted with no general statutory remedy.

Partner recognition is closed at the constitutional level. Articles 49, 50, 51 and 52 of the 1992 Constitution limit marriage, de facto unions and the family to one man and one woman, and Article 140 of the Civil Code expressly prohibits marriage between persons of the same sex. An 8 January 2018 advisory opinion of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights held that states party to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family registration systems, including marriage; Paraguay is a party to the Convention, but its law has not been adapted and a lawsuit relying on the opinion to recognise same-sex marriage remains pending. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no route to marriage or union recognition, and the same gap applies to trans residents.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1990. The age of consent is 16 for homosexual conduct and 14 for heterosexual conduct, a distinction that can bear on a younger trans visitor in a relationship local law reads as same-sex.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American human rights system has pushed further than Paraguayan domestic law. The advisory opinion of 8 January 2018 applies across states party to the American Convention, and Bolivian, Paraguayan and Peruvian law alike recognise neither same-sex marriage nor same-sex unions, so the regional standard sits well ahead of the three jurisdictions' statutes.

Public opinion on same-sex marriage remains among the lowest in South America. A Pew survey conducted between 26 November 2013 and 8 January 2014 recorded 15 per cent support and 81 per cent opposition, and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 26 per cent support. The Catholic Church retains strong institutional influence and has opposed measures to improve LGBT lives, with a rise in religious fundamentalism reported as a concern among advocacy groups. These attitude and religious-influence findings concern LGBT people and same-sex marriage generally rather than trans people specifically.

LGBT groups have organised pride parades in Asunción since 2004.
localsOnly:
Adoption law contains no explicit bar on same-sex couples or single people. Law 1136 of 1997, in force since 1997, does not list sexual orientation or gender identity among its prohibitions, which cover infectious disease, mental disorders and child-abuse records, and single persons of any sex may adopt regardless of marital status. Equal preference is given to opposite-sex marriages and de facto unions and to single women. The gap permits adoption by same-sex couples as couples and by single men or women, within a society that still closes doors to them.

Sectoral protections cover sexual orientation in specific settings without a general non-discrimination statute. Law 5162 of 2014, Article 274 of the Criminal Enforcement Code, requires that sexual orientation be considered alongside age and degree of psychic development when housing adolescents in collective dormitories. Decree 6973 under Law 577 of 2016 protects women in situations of violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation. Law 6149 of 2018 on protection and facilities for naturalisation of stateless persons bars discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Law 6534 of 2020 treats sexual orientation data as sensitive personal data. Article 28 of the internal rules of the Ministry of Public Defense prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation against employees.

There is no official prohibition on the entry of gay, lesbian or bisexual people into the Armed Forces and National Police. In June 2010 the Chamber of Deputies rejected, by 42 votes to 4, a bill that would have prohibited the entry of homosexuals into the Public Force.

The 2016 name lawsuit brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda invokes Article 25 of the Constitution on free expression and the free construction of identity and Article 42 of the Civil Code allowing change of a first name. The constitutional and civil-code arguments available to residents are the same ones a trans visitor would have to rely on, and they have not yet produced a ruling.
outOfScopeNotes:
The ten recognition lawsuits have no final rulings, and the UN Human Rights Committee communications filed by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights are still awaiting a decision. The outcome and any compliance by Paraguay are unresolved.

The lawsuit seeking recognition of a same-sex marriage on the basis of the 8 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion remains pending. Whether the domestic-law gap identified after the opinion will be closed is not sourced.

The November 2015 anti-discrimination bill has not advanced since introduction; no parliamentary schedule or vote is recorded.

Violence data is incomplete for this assessment. The 37 feminicides registered in 2025 are not disaggregated for trans victims, and no trans-specific homicide or violence count with a denominator was located in the source inventory, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made. The two identity-document refusals recorded by Amnesty International are individual cases rather than a count.

The Asunción city council's ban on the event honouring the trans human-rights defender is recorded without the resolution text, the stated grounds or any legal challenge, so whether it rests on a general municipal events rule or on the subject matter of the event is not sourced.
